title: Engage with aesthetic, affective, cultural and social values in texts

lessons.title: Texts that touch our feelings
lessons.html:
What is a text?

A text is any message that people can read, hear or see. A story, a poem, a song, a praise poem (izibongo), a radio drama, a TV programme, a photograph, a mural and even a poster are all texts.

Aesthetic value: beauty

Aesthetic means how beautiful or pleasing something is. We enjoy a song because of its rhythm and melody, a poem because of the sound of the words, and a picture because of its colours. Writers make texts beautiful with:

  • Rhythm and rhyme, like in songs and children's rhymes.
  • Repetition of words or lines, as in many praise poems and church hymns.
  • Images (word pictures), for example: the veld was a brown blanket after the long drought.
  • Comparisons, for example: he is as strong as a bull.

Affective value: feelings

Affective means how a text makes us feel. A story about a family losing their cattle in a drought can make us sad. A song at a wedding makes us happy. A speech can make us proud or angry. Writers choose words to make us feel something.

Reading and listening actively

When you read or listen to a text, ask yourself:

  1. What is it about?
  2. How does it make me feel, and why?
  3. Which words or pictures caused that feeling?
  4. Did I enjoy it? What did I like or not like?

There is not always one right answer. Different people can feel different things about the same text, and that is fine if they can explain why.

lessons.title: Culture and social values in texts
lessons.html:
Texts carry culture

Texts show the culture of the people who made them: their language, beliefs, customs, food, clothes and way of life. South Africa has a rich mix of cultures, and our texts show this.

Examples

  • Praise poems (izibongo, dithoko) honour chiefs, families and heroes and tell their history.
  • Folktales told by grandparents around the fire often use animals, like the clever hare or the greedy hyena, to teach lessons.
  • Proverbs carry wisdom in a few words, for example the Zulu saying umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu (a person is a person through other people), which expresses ubuntu.
  • Songs sung while working, at weddings, at funerals and during the struggle for freedom.
  • Beadwork, murals and crafts, such as Ndebele house painting, are visual texts with meaning.

Social values

Social values are ideas about what is right, wrong and important in a community, such as respect for elders, sharing, honesty, hard work and caring for the land and animals. Texts often teach or question these values. For example, a folktale may show that greed is punished, and a modern song may speak out against crime or gender-based violence.

Thinking about values in a text

  1. What values does the text show? Respect? Courage? Fairness?
  2. Whose voice is heard, and whose voice is missing?
  3. Does the text treat all people fairly, including women, children and people of other cultures?
  4. Do you agree with the values? Why or why not?

Sharing texts at work

On farms people from many cultures work together. Sharing songs, stories and celebrations builds respect and teamwork. Be curious and respectful about other people's culture, and do not mock what you do not understand.

Key points

  • A text is any message people read, hear or see.
  • Aesthetic value is about beauty; affective value is about feelings.
  • Texts carry culture, such as praise poems, folktales and proverbs.
  • Social values are ideas about what is right and important.
  • Think critically about values and respect other cultures.
